blocks.x: Yes, we want to get your name. Could I have your full name?
Yeah, you can have all the names you want.
Okay. What is your name please?
My name is Noah Haywood Cook.
Noah Haywood? Is that H-A-Y?
H-A-Y-W-R-D. Haywood. H-A-Y-W-R-D.

And what is your name? Marjorie Zander. And my name is Dick Allen and we're recording this on Lincoln Court. What is the address here? 2527 Lincoln Court. And let me see, what else I wanted to ask you. Oh, today's date is August the...
August 30th.
30th of August 1960.
Yeah, that's your Long birthday. Is that right? That's right. Celebrating a lot of these places here.
Well now, let's see. I'd like to get your birthday.
Mine, July the 30th, 1879.
And where were you born?
I was born in Leveson Parish. In Leveson Parish. That's where I was born at. But I was raised in Baton Rouge.
Mm-hmm. How old were you when you...

When I left Leveson Parish, I left there, I must have been about... I just can't remember, I must have been about six years old. And I moved over to East Baton Rouge Parish. After I left there... Is that thing taking me now?
Yeah, that's good.

Alright. I left Leveson Parish and moved over to East Baton Rouge Parish. I went to a place they called the Banker Place. My oldest brother, my daddy died, and I was three years old. My oldest brother was taking care of it. And each one of them getting married, the dozen would take my mother. We lived at the Banker Place, say, three years. We moved from there to Charlie Christian Place, about a mile above where we were first living. We'd lain there until I was 11 years old. I moved from there to Baton Rouge at 11 years old. And I mained in Baton Rouge until 1899, when the Spanish-American War broke out. I got a job in the racetrack. I lived there for a year. I got hurt. The day the maine blowed up, I got throated. The horse throated. That's why I wasn't in the first volunteer regiment. After I got well in 1899, the war started in the Philippine Islands. And I came here, and I stayed in the recruiting office from April, May, and June, and July. The first place, I was too young. I wasn't about 19 years old. But I tried to fool the man and tell him I was 21. Well, he didn't accept that. But he said, your weight. I only weighed 95 pounds. And he said, I'm going to keep you here. If you ask me, live in uterine? He said, no, I live in Baton Rouge. He said, I'm going to keep you here and feed you until I get you up to the weight. Alright, I stayed there three months. I got up to the weight. I got the weight up to 105. The doctor come in one morning and called me and the white boys. Called us in and weighed us. Well, I come up to 105. He had about 167 different weights. Alright, and he said, well, I'm on the list of us. He swore me in on the 15th of July, 1899. And he sent me to Texas to accompany the D of the 25th Regiment. I remained there about four months. And I moved from there up to San Antonio, Texas. I actually met San Antonio. I stayed there about three, about four months. Then there was an order to the Philippine Islands. The order came from Washington. And we left San Antonio, Texas on the first day of October, 1900. And we sailed. We got to Hungolula in four days from the time we left. And on October 29th, we landed in Manila Bay. We go a hundred miles from Manila to a place called De Saur. And we stayed there, well, a little over a year. We moved from there to a place they called Moncarta. While we was up there, there's so many goo-goos up there, till the white regiments up there they couldn't uphand them. They sent us up there to get them out of their mountain. And we went up there and we stayed about eight, well, I say a year we stayed there. And we got them all out. The last one camp we got, we take one camp and about a hundred men in it. We captured about ten, killed four, and took all the bolos out. The shotguns, the rifles. They must have had about a hundred rifles in there. And God knows how many bolos. And during that time, I only had about four months to serve. And Lieutenant Charles F. Bates, our commander, and he wanted me to remain in the company. And I asked him, could I take one of them bolos home? For sure to the people. He told me yes. And all them had asked for a bolos that got one, because I had a hundred of them there but didn't know what to do with them. And as we got through with that, on June the 15th, I sailed back to the United States. I arrived in the United States on the 26th day of July, 1902. After 1902, I caught the train, I come home to Baton Rouge. I worked carpentry, worked there for six years. I got tired of working. I went on back down here to Madison Barracks, New York. I mean Madison Barracks here, and re-enlisted. I went to Madison Barracks, New York. I mean that three years and three months. And when that time was out, my regiment went back to the Philippine Islands. But I didn't want to go. I only had three months to serve. And I had to re-enlist if I went back. So I rather stayed. So I stayed in Madison Barracks, two months waiting for the regiment to come from the Philippine Islands to take our place. And after that, I come to New Orleans. I went to Baton Rouge. I see my sister and mother. Then I came here. I landed here on the first day of January, 1913. And I remained single. 1913, 14, 15, 16, 17. 1918, July the 12th. I married Corrine Foster. That's the wife I got now. And I've been in New Orleans ever since. That's the hit.
That's it, huh?
That's it. That's it. That's it.
Well, we wanted to ask you about some of the little games that the children's played. When you were young?

Well, we played, the only thing ever I know to play is baseball. We played ball and played marble. But I never was much of a baseball player. I was a King Marble shot. That was my game. I won all the marbles the boys had in Baton Rouge. It was about, you ain't got no business to come. Go ahead. So I played marbles and tops and everything. That's all I done. Then I formed and made cotton. While I was in Baton Rouge, I made cotton in the country. Because Baton Rouge, the place didn't have much work. And my brother, they worked. My oldest brother was taking care of me. He worked at Lecher, Sawmill. Well, I wasn't old enough to get there. In them days, you couldn't work unless you were 21. You wouldn't get no pay. Let the boys work. And he took the effort whilst I made cotton. And I made cotton for three or four years. And then the cotton went down to five cents a pound and we quit. See? Then he got married. And that ends that story. And now I'm here since 1913.
Did you sing when you made cotton? When you were picking cotton, I ain't?
No. I never was a song singer.
You never did?

I never did do no singing. No. I never did do no singing. No. Our people wasn't much for songs. None of them. My brother was the one that raised me. He could hum a little song now and then. But none of us would know she was singing. None of them.
Do you remember any of the songs that he hummed?
My daughter, she's a good song singer.
No, I mean that your brother hummed. Yeah, no. No, you don't remember.
I'll tell you what I got here, but I couldn't have to write it. I would have written if I had thought about it. I got a song that we hummed and messed around with. It was written some 75 years ago.
Well, how did the words go? Do you remember that?

It goes about the old, John brought old mule. The name was Joe. And nobody could put the saddle on Joe's old mule. Well, I could write that. I'd written that two or three times and they laughed at it. And I tried to get it on record. They laughed at it. But if I had thought about it, she was coming. I didn't think about it. I can write that. But I know it's good, but I can't sing it.
Well, I'd like to just have the words. It sounds like a good song to me. It is. I got to write it.

I'll write it and give it to you. I'll write it and send it to you. I'll do that. And if you make that sing out, let them know. But I'll write it. I can't bring it like now. No. But I had written that twice. I had it in my desk there, but I lost it. And I had these here humming around on it. And they say my daughter, my granddaughter, she was singing for the record. And I tried to get her to sing it. And she said it's too old fashioned. But it's not old fashioned. It's a song that is sung by Villa Kersan. The first Negro minister man in the United States.
Villa Kersan?
That's sung by him. I know a lot of people who worked with him.
Well, then I got it.

I can write that. And then I had two, but one of them is too vulgar. He couldn't make that. He couldn't sing that. I know that's good, but I couldn't write that. But Sam, I can write that to old Mule. And I wish I had written it. And my son, yeah, he could. He's sung it if I had written it. But I'll write it if you tell me to write it and I'll send it to you.
Oh, that's good.

Yeah. Wish I had written that song. I've been wanting to get it on something. I sure would have. I know that. Perfect. We used to hum it and play around with it. And after Villa Kersan come to Baton Rouge once when I was a boy and sung it. And everybody was trying to sing it. And I just got the words in. And I never will forget it. I never will forget it. But I could have written it and had it for you if I thought of it. I didn't think about it.
Well, he sings it.

I'll write it. And I'll send it wherever you say send it. And if you can make anything, it's a good song, all right. It'll take today. You can make a good record out of that song. Yeah. I'll write it up if you can sing.
Well, I think something like that belongs in the university because that's history from 75 years ago.

Oh, it's more than that. I guess 80 years. That's all it's sung. There's a time that Villa Kersan went to Langland and made Queen Victoria live. And then you have queens and kings don't live. But I understand that Villa Kersan made her live to give him a $500 go or a diamond ring. I saw Villa Kersan. The greatest minister man ever after the Negro race, after the Civil War. And he made a hit with that song. And I'll never forget it. And I'll write it. And if I had a thought about it, if I had it written here, my boy can sing it, see. He can sing.
Well, how did he make Queen Victoria laugh?

Acting a fool on the stage. Yeah, acting a fool on the stage. He said that people, them people go to shows, they don't enjoy. Just sat and looked. Too much great to laugh. But he turned her tickling box over. He was a great minister man. Acting a fool on the stage. Well, he made her laugh. Now that was what record we got when I was a young man.
I heard that he took the whole teacup and salsa and put it in his mouth.

Well, I tell you. Now that's, I see, well that was a fella in Texas. We beat him up there once by kicking our lady friend. He wasn't Billika Sam, but he said he was. He came to Texas. And he put billiard balls and he put plates in his mouth. All that. But I never see Billika Sam do that. I saw him on the stage. He just naturally cracked jokes and calm and danced. That's all he had done. He didn't put all that junk in his mouth. But I did see a man in Texas in 1900. He put anything in his mouth. He put it, he, they tell me, now I don't know, but they tell me he made some white women faint in the streetcar. He scared them. He walked in the streetcar and stuck that plate in his mouth and looked at some of them. They're faint. And they ran him away from that. That's where I understood. Now I was in the barracks. I don't know. And we used to come in town to them bar rooms and things while they say they'd run him away. Say he put a, put a plate in his mouth and come in the streetcar with him. And he'd excite some women in his faint.
It seems to me that they had some trouble down there in Texas with his soldiers, didn't they?

No, they had trouble right in Brownsville, Texas. Were you there? My company, no, I was out. I was out. I would have been in it if I had been there. Then my company, when I told them, they saw a brown in Texas.
That's when Teddy Roosevelt was president. Mm-hmm.
That was how...
Teddy Roosevelt had something to do with that.

He sent... Well, Teddy Roosevelt done the right thing. He didn't want to try them down there. If he'd have tried them, all he went to prison. But the fact that he was, well, he just discharged them disarm them. He didn't kick them out. You can get a pension on a, on a, on a, on a discharge without honor. That's the way they were discharged. The whole company just had to leave. And they built the company over again. He said that if they turned them men over to the civil authority, they'd send them all the penitentiary. They would have. Every one of them went to penitentiary. So the men are glad they accept that. They accept that. Get disarm or discharge. Discharge without honor. Of course, my discharge is all honor. I have two in there. There's no black man or white man. You ain't got two like I got. I said six years and four months, three months, without a coat marshal. And brother, you had to be on your toes to keep that, without getting a coat marshal. This army they got there, I called a tin army. They didn't sold it like I did. I had to come through the hole. I had to do it. We didn't play. I went down the barracks one day and I got to talk to an officer. He was down in the Philippines. He was very old, he was fixing his tie. And we were talking about soldiers. I went in his office, the captain down there. And he found out that I was an old ex-solder from 24th. I had to go in his office, me and some of them talk. How we sold it and how these boys sold you. They give you more time in jail. For nothing than regular arm in my day. Man, they kick you out of the army right now. See, so many kicked out. Disarms discharge. But disobeying any order. You can't disobey no order. And that, these fellas down to the back, you had prisoners guarding them. And he was sitting in a wheelbar with his back to the prisoners. And they were out there cutting grass. I said, boy, what you doing? And he says, I'm guarding prisoners. I said, you're back to the prisoners? I said, brother, in my day you'd get 10 months in jail. It was blessed to join that kind of guard duty. So I saw two officers coming. And the center, he got off his post and come over and talked to me. I said, look, boy, there come an officer. What are you going to do? He looked and he saw two officers coming. He went back on his post. And when they passed, he saluted them. And the time they passed, he'd come on back there and sit down. I said, y'all, he said, we just here. We just here. He said, we just here. I said, y'all ain't soldiers. He said, no. We just here. That's all. First time to make out. A green army like that put them in France. It's a shame. I trained six years to handle a rifle. A man can't shoot no gun in no four or five months. He must learn that gun. He got to learn to defend his self. For he'd be a regular target if he didn't learn how to defend himself on the fire line. You got that. You got to learn that. The government learned all them things. You got to know them things. You can't just go to work and feel a man shot a gun and tell him, give him one of them rifles and tell him go out there and load it and he'll jam it. And he'd be out there and the enemy would kill him. Oh, he'd get the thing on jam. See? And you got to know how to load them guns. The one I used, like this militia got there, that's the gun I used in my second enlistment. The first gun I used was an empty cartridge. You put the cartridge in a chamber to the side of the gun and you put five in there. And every time you'd rope that boat and put it back and shove it, the old cartridge would jump out and another one would come in. That's called a Craig Jogerson rifle. That's the one I used in the Philippines. That's the one I used in Cuba. That's the one I used in New York. The same gun that the militia got. Now I got, World War I got a force up there and they got four or five of them. They give them to them to drill with them.
Is that the Springfield 03? Is that it? Yeah. Is that the Springfield 03?

Yeah, all of them. They got about six. I bet they got seven, eight of them guns up there. We could have got them, but we was too old. Our men are dying too fast. We were too old to get them, Teddy Rose, Teddy Rose, Teddy Rose, all the organization sold us to get them guns because they disqualified them in the regular hours. And the guns now they got is not near as good as that gun there. Them guns there, I know what they'll do. I would never kill you 2,300 yards and show you living. I know that myself. They can't tell me they won't, they will. Them old crack Jogerson rifles would kill you 2,500 yards. You stand there and they can kill you so far with them, that rifle, because you couldn't hear the sound. All you could hear was that bullet when it hit. That's right. I know them guns. So, after I got out of the service, they didn't want me to leave, but I tell you, I thought six years and something was longer than that. I could have retired at 55, from the time I went in. But the laws, the laws were too strict. I was afraid I'd get in jail. And I didn't want to get in no government jail. They were hard on us. So, when I got my time out, I left. Come here and hung around here a few months and got married. But I didn't intend to stay here. My intention was to go back to Springfield, Ohio and get married there. My brother. Well, my brother was here then. He was living on the Marnie Street. I got here with him. He begged me to stay. I was always gone for my people. I never saw one of my people buried yet but him. I saw the only one, all my people dead, and the only one ever I saw buried was my brother I buried there last year. I would have read them died. I wasn't around. I was reading New York or in the Philippines somewhere. Two brothers died while I was in the Philippine Islands. One sister-in-law died. Yeah, I saw my sister. Two of my people. Out of seven of those, I saw two buried. My sister died. Yeah buried there. Yeah and my brother died. So that's that.
Well, in those days, how long could they keep somebody? 24 hours.

Before they buried him. Yes, sir. No sister, you keep no weekend. No, you couldn't. If you died today, they buried you tomorrow. Out of that. Now, there's stuff that's stuff that's stinging you there and keep you in mind. But them days you didn't. If you died tonight, they buried you the next day. Yes, for them old men in the country and I was a boy and nobody died, they'd be getting out of their shovels and get down to the grave or dig that grave. And buried you. No, no keeping it. And then they'd preach funer like they do now at the church house. How much Christians you had, they wouldn't carry no church. They'd carry you in the burial. And one year after you was dead, they'd preach your funeral. That was the way it was done in them days. Now they carry it to the church and preach your funeral and that's ended. But not in them days. No. No. And then the education qualification. They tell you something about that. The black people in that day didn't have much of a school in them. The first time ever I went to school, I went to a white woman, Ms. Cardwell. All I went from now, come up to get school age 75 years ago, there wasn't no colored teachers. All white. There was two or three more men my age and I know that I'm telling the truth. I went to a white woman. She'd teach me to my ABCs up until I was, I went there about a year. And after the first colored man come there, Professor Levi, he came. Then another one come called Professor Page. And that's why the white folks began to give over. The woman I went to school, she left, went back to New York. Well, it's the company. They're all companies and all. But we had no colored schools in them days. So now the first preschool to open up, after the first preschool in Baton Rouge opened up, then Professor Levi was put in charge of it. Then Roy went there for nothing after preschool them days. That's when the first opened up. There wasn't no preschool before that. Used to be 10 cents a week. And Miss Cartwright, she, oh, she had about, oh man, she must have had about seven or eight of children. Had a great big shed in the back. And a whole lot of desks, black boys. And she teached us from that. And that's where I left. And I left her, I could read in the, I could read in the first reading. When I went to preschool, well I know I could read that well. And after the preschool, the preacher, the message preacher comes, he had an education. He opened up a school. And that's where I went there. But the most, what I do know, I got it through the Army. You see, you had to go to school in the Army. We had to go to school. We had to go to the Nunca Mitchell School. And the chapter in the 25th or the 24th, they teach school. And you had to read, you had to know how to read and write. They'd say that. You come up there, couldn't spare a check, they'd go and send you to school. See? So I went to school there. If I had kept on with the chapter, I'd have been more than eighth grade. I think I'm about eighth grade now. But I could have gotten higher than that, but I didn't study. I wanted to be out in town with other boys. I didn't go to school. So far as Nunca Mitchell School, I had to go there. I had to go there.
You were a non-commissioned officer? Huh?
You were a non-commissioned officer?
I know, I, yeah.

I was a carpenter. I was a carpenter. I made carpenter the second year after I did that. I was a carpenter. I was surprised I got there, I didn't stay. I'd have been a child if I stayed, if I didn't stay. See, I was a non-commissioned officer the second year after I got there. And we used to have a non-commissioned officer school every Wednesday. And I used to ask, you see, an elected man can't do no talking to officers. He can't, he said, that's all he can do to shoot your officers and go. He can't do no talking. But in that school, you can ask, you can talk to them. It's like I'm talking to you. So I remember one day I was coming to Watertown, New York. And I had a second lieutenant coming out of West Park. He sent him to us. So I was coming down the sidewalk. And when I got to the, before I showed him the colonel's house, he had a force to the colonel. The first sergeant was standing on the ground. And he sees me saluting. And he said, who that dude was with? I said, that's the lieutenant. And they said, lieutenant? Well, I hope we won't get him. I said, well, we didn't get him. Because I didn't like him to the second lieutenant in the regular hours. They didn't want a soldier on me. It was too hard. I hope we won't get him. So we didn't get him. But anyway, on that fallen, on the fallen Wednesday, we had none commissioned all to school. He had to come to school. He had to come to school. You know. So my captain was in Greenville, Mississippi, Captain R.J. Mikesville. So I asked in the school, my captain, he was a head teacher in the school, so he was a captain in the force. And I asked Captain Mikesville, I asked that lieutenant, I said, where did you come from? He told me, he said, I come from South Carolina. And then I said, well, I thought so. And that made the whole school laugh. They wanted to know why you asked him. I said, well, I wanted to know. So the captain, I said, after he got to see with the lad, they said, well, the captain, he said, why are you asking that for? I said, well, I'll tell you what. I said, I'm on my fourth year in the regular hours. And every time I get an officer, I told you I'd come from Newtown, Mississippi, Texas. And I said, I want to know why. He said, the captain, he tickled him. He's a nice man. He said, well, I'll tell you. The water partner says, the white folks in the South know us better than the people in the North. That's what he said. The more folks who live together, they know us better. That's why. They gives us. Now, I said, that's what I wanted to know. Why, they all sent us all the sudden out there. Now, he was from Greensboro, Mississippi. All Southern North, those black regiment. All them three regiment went into existence. All Southern North.
But do you think you would have gotten along better with North? No.

I thought, no. That's the question he asked me. I told him, no. I didn't think he'd get along any better with Captain. I said, here's what I figured. I said, the, the, the, the blueback book tells us what we have to do towards the office, and the office has got to tell us what we got to do towards ourselves. So, therefore, it wouldn't be no better. It would be the same thing, but I just wanted to know. That's all. I said, the book guides the army. He said, that's right. The book guides the army. Now, in, in, uh, making the, in the drill, I had the, I made a furlough. Now, if you've got ten points on every question you answered, you get ten points. And when you've got thirty points, you've got a furlough. And I made my thirty points to answer questions. And I'd ask anything I wanted to know in the commission office to. One time, the officer asked me, he says, now this is 1910. The airships hadn't exist. He says to me, if I had a squad on the prairie ground out there, and my airships lit down there. What did you do? I said, when? Twenty-five years from now or? From tomorrow night. He said, tomorrow night. I said, I'd run. He said, that's right. I said, I'd take my squad and run. He said, nothing like that exists at that time. Of course, I had a ship in 1910. And that's why I tried to fly from here. I wasn't here. He tried to fly from there to the kennel and fell. That's the kennel and killed himself.
That's my son, huh?

Yeah. That's from here. That's why I kept it. Wasn't existing then. So the world, I've been in here a long time. And I don't know so much about the other fella, but I know for myself. Well, you have a good memory.
You remember everything very good. I can remember anything. It was a little boy.
I heard a fella say once when he was a little boy, he can remember when he colored the steps and pulled back. But I can't remember that. No, I can't remember.
But I can remember everything.

My mind is just a clear night, wasn't as funny as it is. You know how I can? I never take a drink of liquor in my life. Is that right? Never take a drink of beer or liquor since I've been in the world. Now, a man that drinks, when he gets my age, he gets two. That's right.
Your brain bound to affect your brain.

Alcohol. Bound to affect you. Because so far as me, I never took a drink in my life. The only thing I drank is some of these pop here, the junk you got here. Sometimes I drink it and then times I don't.
I guess they didn't have Coca-Cola when you were a little.

No, nothing like that. You used to have a drink in the Florida called Pop. And had a big hard that he didn't put in that thick bottle. It would bust. It would bust the bottle. And you take it and you pull it like that and the cork would jump out. Called it Pop. While we used to drink that sometimes. But the liquor and beer, I never did drink.
What did that pop taste like? It tastes like lemonade.

Just about like lemonade. Yeah, different flavor. Because when I did drink, I used to drink it. I used to drink it to the white time. It tastes like lemonade. Yeah. Then the age would get, we would get a guy and a whiskey to pick this. And he had to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to get a guy and a whiskey to Thank you.

I can talk about Bible, I can talk about...I'll tell you what I can talk about. 1897 I was working on the plantation down at the Guides White Castle. And I had a brother in the swamp, not a brother, but a first cousin in the swamp. And he wanted me to come and see. Well, I told him I didn't have no pistols. He said, don't you come to that dog's pistols. I never ever owned a pistol in my life. And I went to that, I bought one of those swamp engine pistols, paid three dollars for it. Now I had to go through a swamp, cause there's plenty of bears in the swamp. And he says to me, he said, now if you run into a bear...
Tell me about Chalmette. How long have you been going down there?

1928. All the Civil War died out. And we took over. We took over. After we took over, we've been going ever since. When they made a national park out of it, we got a letter from the head of that park that continued that graveyard. Don't have to key in it. Just continued the graveyard every year. As long as any of us lived. And when we all died out, to give it to World War I. So World War I now is running it. But I miss the head dog in the show. Because I go and give over to us. And there ain't but 14 of us living. And they're not able to attend. So I take that their part.
Right on there. Let's look at... Huh? Wait, let me get... Alright. This is a picture you say of the men who used to run Chalmette.
That picture that we run it. Now they ain't but four that's on that living. All the rest of them dead.
Well one man has his wife there with him or something.
No, that's a nurse.
A nurse. And she was in the thing.
Yeah, she was a nurse in Cuba in 1898. She's dead.
And one fella's still got his hat on I see. Well he's dead. He's got his hat from that time.
